title: Linear Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
This report demonstrates a complete linear regression workflow:
Explore Data → Specify Models → Estimate Models → Compare Models → Evaluate Assumptions → Select a Model → Interpret Results
We will use the carData::Prestige dataset to investigate associations between occupational prestige, education, income, and occupational category.
Our objectives are to:

Specify and estimate several plausible competing regression models.
Compare nested models using F-tests and changes in explained variance.
Evaluate overall model performance using R², adjusted R², and RMSE.
Examine regression diagnostics.
Select and interpret a preferred model.
Report results reproducibly using Quarto.

All numerical results in this document are generated directly from the analysis.

title: Linear Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
section: 1. Load packages and prepare the data
text:
1. Load packages and prepare the data
Install any missing packages once in the R Console:
install.packages(c(
  "carData", "dplyr", "tidyr", "ggplot2",
  "broom", "performance", "gt"
))
The following code belongs in the Quarto document.


Code
library(carData)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(broom)
library(performance)
library(gt)

# Keep the same complete-case sample for every model
dat <- Prestige |>
  select(prestige, education, income, type) |>
  drop_na() |>
  mutate(type = factor(type))

n <- nrow(dat)


The dataset contains occupational prestige scores, average education, average income, and occupational categories.
We use complete cases for all variables so that the candidate models are estimated using the same observations.
The final analysis includes 98 occupations.

Research question and predictions
How are education, income, and occupational category associated with occupational prestige?
We expect:

Occupations requiring more education to have higher prestige.
Occupations with higher average incomes to have higher prestige.
Occupational category to explain additional variation in prestige beyond education and income.

These are predictions about associations, not causal effects.

title: Linear Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
3. Specify and estimate competing models
We will fit an intercept-only model and three increasingly complex substantive models.








Model
Formula
Research rationale




M0: Null
prestige ~ 1
Baseline model


M1: Education
prestige ~ education
Prestige varies with education


M2: Education + Income
prestige ~ education + income
Income explains additional variation


M3: Expanded
prestige ~ education + income + type
Occupational category explains additional variation



The models are nested: each successive model contains all predictors from the preceding model, plus one or more additional predictors.


Code
# Intercept-only model
mod0 <- lm(prestige ~ 1, data = dat)

# Education model
mod1 <- lm(prestige ~ education, data = dat)

# Education + income model
mod2 <- lm(prestige ~ education + income, data = dat)

# Expanded model
mod3 <- lm(prestige ~ education + income + type, data = dat)



Inspecting the models
After executing the model-fitting code, explore the results in the R Console:
summary(mod0)
summary(mod1)
summary(mod2)
summary(mod3)

confint(mod3)
Some important interpretive distinctions:

In M0, the intercept represents the sample mean prestige score.
In M1, the education coefficient represents the expected difference in prestige associated with one additional year of average education.
In M2, the education coefficient represents this association after adjusting for income.
In M3, education and income coefficients are additionally adjusted for occupational category.

For categorical predictors, R uses a reference category by default.
Examine the coding using:
levels(dat$type)
contrasts(dat$type)

title: Linear Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
4. Compare the models
We will evaluate the models using two complementary approaches.
Nested-model F-tests determine whether the additional predictor(s) in a larger model produce a statistically significant improvement in fit.
Overall model performance describes how well each model fits the observed data.
Our main performance metrics are:

R²: Proportion of variation explained.
Adjusted R²: Explained variation adjusted for model complexity.
RMSE: Root mean squared error, expressed in prestige-score units.
ΔR²: Increase in explained variation compared with the preceding model.


4.1. Conduct nested-model comparisons
Because our models are nested and estimated using the same observations, we can compare all four models in a single anova() call.


Code
tests <- anova(mod0, mod1, mod2, mod3)

tests


Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: prestige ~ 1
Model 2: prestige ~ education
Model 3: prestige ~ education + income
Model 4: prestige ~ education + income + type
  Res.Df     RSS Df Sum of Sq        F    Pr(>F)    
1     97 28346.9                                    
2     96  7064.4  1   21282.5 422.8056 < 2.2e-16 ***
3     95  5272.4  1    1792.0  35.5999 4.355e-08 ***
4     93  4681.3  2     591.2   5.8721  0.003966 ** 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Each row represents a model. The F-statistic and p-value on each row after the first test whether that model improves fit relative to the preceding model.
For example:

M1 versus M0 tests the contribution of education.
M2 versus M1 tests the additional contribution of income.
M3 versus M2 tests the joint additional contribution of occupational category.

We can retain and rename the statistics relevant to our comparison table.


Code
tests <- tests |>
  select(Res.Df, Df, F, `Pr(>F)`) |>
  rename(
    Residual.df = Res.Df,
    Nested.Df = Df,
    Nested.F.stat = F,
    Nested.p.value = `Pr(>F)`
  )




4.2. Extract overall model performance
The glance() function returns a one-row data frame containing model-level statistics.
We can apply it to each fitted model.


Code
glance0 <- glance(mod0)
glance1 <- glance(mod1)
glance2 <- glance(mod2)
glance3 <- glance(mod3)


We can then combine these results using rbind().


Code
mods <- c(
  "M0: Null",
  "M1: Education",
  "M2: + Income",
  "M3: + Type"
)

glances <- rbind(
  glance0,
  glance1,
  glance2,
  glance3
)




4.3. Combine nested tests and model performance
Because the rows in glances and tests represent the same models in the same order, we can combine them using cbind().


Code
comparison_table <- cbind(
  Model = mods,
  glances,
  tests
)


Next, calculate the change in R² between successive models using lag().
We will also calculate RMSE directly from each model’s residuals.


Code
comparison_table <- comparison_table |>
  mutate(
    Delta.R2 = r.squared - lag(r.squared),

    RMSE = c(
      sqrt(mean(residuals(mod0)^2)),
      sqrt(mean(residuals(mod1)^2)),
      sqrt(mean(residuals(mod2)^2)),
      sqrt(mean(residuals(mod3)^2))
    )
  ) |>
  select(
    Model,
    r.squared,
    Delta.R2,
    adj.r.squared,
    RMSE,
    Residual.df,
    Nested.Df,
    Nested.F.stat,
    Nested.p.value
  )


Why calculate RMSE separately?
Although glance() provides a statistic called sigma, this is the residual standard error rather than the ordinary in-sample RMSE. The two use different denominators.
For consistency, we calculate RMSE explicitly as the square root of the mean squared residual.


4.4. Display the combined model-comparison table


Code
comparison_table |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    Model = "Model",
    r.squared = "R²",
    Delta.R2 = "ΔR²",
    adj.r.squared = "Adjusted R²",
    RMSE = "RMSE",
    Residual.df = "Residual df",
    Nested.Df = "Nested df",
    Nested.F.stat = "Nested F",
    Nested.p.value = "Nested p"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      r.squared,
      Delta.R2,
      adj.r.squared,
      RMSE,
      Nested.F.stat
    ),
    decimals = 3
  ) |>
  fmt(
    columns = Nested.p.value,
    fns = function(x) {
      ifelse(
        is.na(x),
        "—",
        ifelse(x < .001, "< .001", sprintf("%.3f", x))
      )
    }
  ) |>
  sub_missing(
    columns = c(Delta.R2, Nested.Df, Nested.F.stat),
    missing_text = "—"
  )

Interpreting the combined table
Each row represents one fitted model.
The first set of statistics describes the overall performance of that model:

R²
Adjusted R²
RMSE

The second set describes its incremental improvement relative to the preceding model:

ΔR²
Nested degrees of freedom
Nested F-statistic
Nested p-value

For example, the M2 row tells us:

How much variation M2 explains overall.
How much additional variation M2 explains compared with M1.
Whether the improvement is statistically significant.

The M3 comparison tests the joint contribution of occupational category after accounting for education and income.
The M0 row has no incremental comparison because it serves as the baseline.


4.5. Additional performance comparison
The performance package also provides a convenient way to compare fitted models.


Code
performance_comparison <- compare_performance(
  mod0,
  mod1,
  mod2,
  mod3,
  rank = TRUE
)


In the Console, inspect:
performance_comparison
plot(performance_comparison)
These functions may include additional metrics such as AIC and BIC, which we will not focus on here.

title: Linear Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
5. Select a provisional model
Model selection requires considering both statistical evidence and model complexity.
In particular, we should consider:

Whether adding predictors significantly improves model fit.
How much additional variation is explained.
Whether adjusted R² improves.
Whether RMSE meaningfully decreases.
Whether the added complexity is substantively justified.

For this demonstration, we will use adjusted R² as an initial selection criterion.
This is a convenient teaching example, not a universal rule for selecting regression models.


Code
selected_row <- comparison_table |>
  slice_max(
    order_by = adj.r.squared,
    n = 1,
    with_ties = FALSE
  )

selected_name <- selected_row$Model

selected_model <- switch(
  selected_name,
  "M0: Null" = mod0,
  "M1: Education" = mod1,
  "M2: + Income" = mod2,
  "M3: + Type" = mod3
)


The provisionally selected model is M3: + Type.
Its performance is:

R² = 0.835
Adjusted R² = 0.828
RMSE = 6.91 prestige points.

We will now examine whether the selected model has important diagnostic problems.

title: Linear Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
6. Evaluate regression diagnostics
Regression diagnostics help identify potential violations of model assumptions and unusual observations.
We will examine:

Linearity.
Residual normality.
Heteroscedasticity.
Influential observations.
Multicollinearity, where applicable.


Standard diagnostic plots


Code
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 2))

plot(selected_model)





Regression diagnostic plots for the provisionally selected model




Code
par(op)


When interpreting these plots, consider:
Residuals versus fitted values
Is there evidence of curvature or systematic patterns?
Normal Q–Q plot
Do the residuals deviate substantially from a normal distribution?
Scale–location plot
Does residual variability change across fitted values?
Residuals versus leverage
Are there observations with unusually high leverage or influence?


Additional diagnostics
The performance package provides a more comprehensive diagnostic interface.
Run the following interactively in the Console:
check_model(selected_model)
For models with multiple predictors, you can also investigate multicollinearity:
check_collinearity(selected_model)
These diagnostics should inform your final model selection.
A model with slightly better fit statistics may not be preferable if its assumptions are seriously compromised.
For the purposes of this worked example, we retain the provisionally selected model for the reporting demonstration.

title: Linear Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
7. Report the selected model

7.1. Extract regression coefficients
The tidy() function extracts coefficient-level results from a fitted model.


Code
coefficient_results <- tidy(
  selected_model,
  conf.int = TRUE,
  conf.level = 0.95
)


The resulting data frame contains:

Coefficient estimates.
Standard errors.
Test statistics.
p-values.
Confidence interval limits.



7.2. Create a regression coefficient table


Code
coefficient_results |>
  select(
    term,
    estimate,
    std.error,
    conf.low,
    conf.high,
    p.value
  ) |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(
    term = "Predictor",
    estimate = "Estimate",
    std.error = "SE",
    conf.low = "95% CI lower",
    conf.high = "95% CI upper",
    p.value = "p"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(
      estimate,
      std.error,

    fns = function(x) {

title: Linear Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
8. Interpret the results

Overall model performance
The selected model, M3: + Type, explains approximately 83.5% of the variation in occupational prestige within this sample.
Its adjusted R² is 0.828, and its in-sample RMSE is 6.91 prestige points.
The RMSE describes the typical magnitude of the model’s fitted residuals on a root-mean-square scale.
It should not be interpreted as an estimate of out-of-sample predictive accuracy.


Interpreting education
Holding the other predictors constant, a one-year increase in an occupation’s average education is associated with a significant 3.67-point increase in predicted occupational prestige, 95% CI [2.4, 4.95].


Interpreting income
Holding the other predictors constant, a one-unit increase in an occupation’s average income is associated with a significant 0.001-point increase in predicted occupational prestige, 95% CI [0.001, 0.001].


Interpreting occupational category
If the selected model includes type, its coefficients represent differences in predicted prestige relative to the reference occupational category, holding constant education and income.
These are adjusted group differences, not differences between the raw category means.


Substantive conclusions
This analysis illustrates how occupational prestige can be investigated using several competing regression models.
The model-comparison process allows us to evaluate whether additional predictors explain meaningful variation beyond simpler models.
The final model provides estimates of the conditional associations between occupational characteristics and prestige.
However, several limitations should be recognized:

The observations describe occupations rather than individual people.
The data are observational.
Regression coefficients represent associations rather than causal effects.
Model diagnostics may reveal limitations not captured by summary fit statistics.
In-sample model performance does not establish out-of-sample predictive accuracy.

Figure 1 shows the approximately normal distribution and density curve of occupational rating scores with a slight left skew.





Figure 1.




Figures 2-4 show the relationships between overall workplace rating and several continuous variables. The handling of complaints, availability of learning opportunities, and satisfaction with raises all appear relatively linear in their relationships with workplace rating, though there may be a slight downward curve in the relationship between rating and raises.





Figure 2.









Figure 3.









Figure 4.




These results are fairly consistent with expectations. Most overall rating scores are centrally clustered, and positive workplace rating is associated with positive scores for the handling of workplace complaints, the provision of learning opportunities, and the availability of pay raises.








The handling of employee complaints is likely to be associated with positive workplace ratings because when complaints are properly addressed, factors that may be lowering workplace rating may disappear or have a lesser impact on overall employee workplace rating. Accounting for the addressing of complaints, opportunities for learning could explain low workplace rating from employees who feel that they are not personally gaining knowledge or experience from their position as opposed to those with interpersonal or workplace issues. Finally, pay increases could account for variation in individuals who are particularly ambitious, financially motivated, or working with bosses who do not pay them enough. Additionally, those with low satisfaction in the handling of complaints and opportunities to learn may still provide an overall rating that is higher than expected when the pay is high enough. It is possible that this data could be skewed due to the sample being from actively employed individuals; those with extremely low workplace satisfaction are more likely to leave their workplace.






Model 0’s coefficient for the intercept represents the sample mean rating score of 64.63. Introducing continuous variables changes the meaning of the coefficients; model 1’s coefficient for complaints, 0.75, indicates the rate at which overall rating points change with the rating of the handling of complaints. Model 2’s coefficient for complaints is 0.64, which does not represent the rate of change in the overall variables, but instead the difference between the results of Model 1 and Model 2, as the second considers yet another variable. This pattern continues in Model 3, where the complaints coefficient also represents the change between Models 2 and 3.

Models 2 and 3 explain the most variance within the dataset overall according to R²; the ΔR² value shows that adding the second predictor, Learning, increased the statistical significance of the model only marginally, and the third, Raises, did not cause any improvement whatsoever. Thus, the predictor Complaints explains much of the observed variation, and Complaints + Learning explains the most variation. The change in root mean squared error (RMSE) show that the most meaningful change in model quality happens with the first predictor being added, with little change with the second and none with the third.






Figure 5 shows the degree of this data’s coherence to assumptions required for linear modeling.





Figure 5.




While there are some cases of divergence, such as in homogeneity of variance, in general the dataset is approximately linear and normal, with somewhat consistent variability of residuals and few influential observations. The only potential problem on a larger scale is the homogeneity of variance; this result shows that variance is somewhat clustered and not even throughout the dataset. However, as the other conditions are met and the statistics show that Model 2 is a good fit otherwise (Table 2), I do not believe that this will effect my findings in a significant way.









I selected the model M2: … + Learning.
Its performance is:

R² = 0.708
Adjusted R² = 0.686
RMSE = 6.47 (rating)

In context of the data, this result indicates that 68.6% of the variation present in overall employee workplace ratings can be explained by the distribution and variation in ratings of the handling of workplace complaints and of the provision of learning opportunities in conjunction. On average, the model’s predicted rating values are around 6.48 rating points away from actual observed rating values; there are 6.48 rating points of error in this model.
This model is more appropriate than models 0, 1, and 3 because it has the highest unique R² value and the highest adjusted R² value. While the introduction of the variable learning was able to explain only a small amount of the variation, model 3 (with the introduction of the raises variable) explained no additional variation beyond complaints and learning. Thus, model 3 only introduces more risk of collinearity with unnecessary variables that explain little variation. While RMSE does increase very slightly in Model 2 compared to Model 3, the difference is so slight that it does not warrant taking the risk. Moreover, as shown in Figure 5, Model 2 fits the majority of the assumptions required for linear modeling.

This data shows that when the rating for the handling of workplace complaints and the rating for learning opportunities are scored at 0 points, the predicted overall workplace rating is 9.87 (intercept). The increase in rating of complaints handling is positively associated with a 9.87, 0.64, 0.21-rating point increase in overall workplace rating if the rating for learning is being held constant. The p-value for this finding is less than 0.001 and the confidence interval is entirely positive, meaning that we are reasonably certain that this is a significant relationship. Similarly, an increase in rating of learning opportunties is positivelt associated with an additional 0.21-rating point increase in overall workplace rating. However, with a p-value at 0.128 and a confidence interval that includes a zero (which would indicate no relationship), we are not confident that this is a statistically significant association.
Overall, these results indicate that the handling of complaints, provision of learning opportunities, and pay raises are all positively associated with overall employee workplace rating, but that complaint handling and learning opportunities can explain much of the variation in overall rating. However, we are more confident in the significance of the complaints variable than the learning opportunities variable. More data may be helpful in the future to further tease out the drivers behind workplace rating.

title: Linear Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
The handling of employee complaints is likely to be associated with positive workplace ratings because when complaints are properly addressed, factors that may be lowering workplace rating may disappear or have a lesser impact on overall employee workplace rating. Accounting for the addressing of complaints, opportunities for learning could explain low workplace rating from employees who feel that they are not personally gaining knowledge or experience from their position as opposed to those with interpersonal or workplace issues. Finally, pay increases could account for variation in individuals who are particularly ambitious, financially motivated, or working with bosses who do not pay them enough. Additionally, those with low satisfaction in the handling of complaints and opportunities to learn may still provide an overall rating that is higher than expected when the pay is high enough. It is possible that this data could be skewed due to the sample being from actively employed individuals; those with extremely low workplace satisfaction are more likely to leave their workplace.






Model 0’s coefficient for the intercept represents the sample mean rating score of 64.63. Introducing continuous variables changes the meaning of the coefficients; model 1’s coefficient for complaints, 0.75, indicates the rate at which overall rating points change with the rating of the handling of complaints. Model 2’s coefficient for complaints is 0.64, which does not represent the rate of change in the overall variables, but instead the difference between the results of Model 1 and Model 2, as the second considers yet another variable. This pattern continues in Model 3, where the complaints coefficient also represents the change between Models 2 and 3.

Models 2 and 3 explain the most variance within the dataset overall according to R²; the ΔR² value shows that adding the second predictor, Learning, increased the statistical significance of the model only marginally, and the third, Raises, did not cause any improvement whatsoever. Thus, the predictor Complaints explains much of the observed variation, and Complaints + Learning explains the most variation. The change in root mean squared error (RMSE) show that the most meaningful change in model quality happens with the first predictor being added, with little change with the second and none with the third.

While there are some cases of divergence, such as in homogeneity of variance, in general the dataset is approximately linear and normal, with somewhat consistent variability of residuals and few influential observations. However, as the other conditions are met and the statistics show that Model 2 is a good fit otherwise (Table 2), I do not believe that this will effect my findings in a significant way.

title: Linear Regression: Model Specification, Comparison, and Interpretation
text:
I selected the model M2: … + Learning.
Its performance is:

R² = 0.708
Adjusted R² = 0.686
RMSE = 6.47 (rating)

In context of the data, this result indicates that 68.6% of the variation present in overall employee workplace ratings can be explained by the distribution and variation in ratings of the handling of workplace complaints and of the provision of learning opportunities in conjunction. On average, the model’s predicted rating values are around 6.48 rating points away from actual observed rating values; there are 6.48 rating points of error in this model.
This model is more appropriate than models 0, 1, and 3 because it has the highest unique R² value and the highest adjusted R² value. While the introduction of the variable learning was able to explain only a small amount of the variation, model 3 (with the introduction of the raises variable) explained no additional variation beyond complaints and learning. Thus, model 3 only introduces more risk of collinearity with unnecessary variables that explain little variation. While RMSE does increase very slightly in Model 2 compared to Model 3, the difference is so slight that it does not warrant taking the risk. Moreover, as shown in Figure 5, Model 2 fits the majority of the assumptions required for linear modeling.

This data shows that when the rating for the handling of workplace complaints and the rating for learning opportunities are scored at 0 points, the predicted overall workplace rating is 9.87 (intercept). The increase in rating of complaints handling is positively associated with a 9.87, 0.64, 0.21-rating point increase in overall workplace rating if the rating for learning is being held constant. The p-value for this finding is less than 0.001 and the confidence interval is entirely positive, meaning that we are reasonably certain that this is a significant relationship. Similarly, an increase in rating of learning opportunties is positivelt associated with an additional 0.21-rating point increase in overall workplace rating. However, with a p-value at 0.128 and a confidence interval that includes a zero (which would indicate no relationship), we are not confident that this is a statistically significant association.
Overall, these results indicate that the handling of complaints, provision of learning opportunities, and pay raises are all positively associated with overall employee workplace rating, but that complaint handling and learning opportunities can explain much of the variation in overall rating. However, we are more confident in the significance of the complaints variable than the learning opportunities variable. More data may be helpful in the future to further tease out the drivers behind workplace rating.
